books.section: Topic 1.3 European exploration in the Americas
The Early Colonial Era: Spain Colonizes the New World

primary_sources: Bartolome de las Casas, A Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies (1542); German edition (1665)

options.text: Rival European powers printed them as anti-Spanish propaganda amid imperial competition
The Spanish crown printed them to publicize its own colonial reforms
options.misconception: The crown had no interest in advertising its own cruelty; the images were printed by its rivals.

options.text: Native American leaders printed them to appeal for European military aid
options.misconception: No such appeals existed; the images were produced by Europeans for European audiences.

options.text: Catholic missionaries printed them to recruit clergy and funding for the American missions
options.misconception: The images appeared in Protestant northern European editions, not in missionary recruitment.

rationales.general:
1. Picture a weapon changing hands. Las Casas wrote in Spanish in 1542 to reform Spain; a century later his words were printed in German, in Protestant northern Europe.
2. Ask who held the weapon now. Not Spain, and not missionaries, but Spain's rivals in the race for empire.
3. Ask what the weapon did. Images of Spanish cruelty made Spain look unfit to rule an empire.
4. Rule out the others. Spain would not advertise its own cruelty, and missionaries did not print German propaganda editions.
Remember: when a source crosses a border and a century, ask who gains from printing it.
rationales.A: The book was printed in German, in Protestant northern Europe, a century after Las Casas wrote. Spain's rivals used his account to discredit Spain while competing with it for empire.
rationales.B: The Spanish crown would not print images of its own cruelty. These editions came from Spain's rivals, not from Spain.
rationales.C: No Native American leaders printed these editions. The images were produced by Europeans for European audiences.
rationales.D: The editions were printed in Protestant northern Europe, not by Catholic missionaries seeking clergy or funds.

stem: The image above is the title page of a 1665 German edition of Las Casas's writings, printed in Protestant northern Europe more than a century after Las Casas wrote. What does the place and date of publication suggest about the purpose of images like this one?

stimulus.text: Title page of a 1665 German edition of Bartolome de las Casas's writings about Spanish actions in the Americas. The title page is in German, the book was printed in northern Europe, and the scenes around the title show Spanish soldiers attacking Indigenous people and forcing them to carry goods. Las Casas wrote his account in Spanish in 1542.
